title: Hunan Farmhouse Pork with Blistered Green Chilies
blurb: Thin-sliced pork seared hard and tossed with wok-blistered chilies, fermented black beans, and a hail of crunchy chili onion.

ingredients.item: 1 lb pork shoulder or thick-cut boneless pork chops
6 long green Anaheim or Hatch chilies, seeded and cut on a sharp bias
2 tbsp salted fermented black beans, rinsed and roughly chopped (or black bean garlic sauce)
1 tbsp Chinese black vinegar or rice vinegar
Neutral oil, kosher salt, black pepper

steps.text: Put the pork in the freezer for 10 minutes to firm up, then slice it against the grain as thin as you can manage. Toss the slices with 1 tbsp of the soy sauce and a heavy grind of black pepper.
steps.tip: Half-frozen meat is the only way to get paper-thin slices with a home knife.

steps.text: Set a carbon steel or heavy stainless skillet over your highest heat and let it preheat dry for 2 minutes, until the surface looks dull and the first wisp of smoke lifts off. Slice the chilies, garlic, and ginger while it heats.
steps.tip: Open a window before you blister chilies.

steps.text: Add a slick of oil and lay the pork out in a single layer. Sear undisturbed for 3 minutes, until the edges curl and the undersides are brown and lacquered, then toss once and scrape it onto a plate.
steps.tip: Two batches beats one crowded gray one.

steps.text: Add another spoonful of oil and dump in the chilies. Leave them mostly alone over high heat for 4 minutes, until the skins are streaked black and blistered and the flesh has slumped.
Push the chilies to one side, add the garlic, ginger, and fermented black beans to the bare metal, and stir for 1 minute until the garlic goes pale gold and the whole pan smells salty and savory.
steps.tip: Any darker than gold and the garlic turns bitter.

steps.text: Return the pork and its juices, add the remaining soy sauce, the vinegar, and the sugar, and toss hard for 2 minutes until the liquid has nearly vanished and everything wears a glossy coat. Heat the jasmine rice in the microwave while you toss.
Kill the heat and fold in the scallion batons and the Crunchy Chili Onion so the crunch survives. Pile it over the hot rice and spoon the pan drippings on top.
steps.tip: Adding chili onion off-heat keeps the fried garlic bits crisp.

swap: If Hatch or Anaheim chilies are gone, use shishitos or a mix of poblano and jalapeno for the same blistered sweetness and heat.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days refrigerated; reheat in a ripping-hot dry skillet, or chop it into leftover rice with a beaten egg for fried rice.

title: Chettinad Pepper Chicken with Curry Leaves
blurb: Chicken thighs browned in coconut oil and coated in a coarse fennel-and-black-pepper masala that crackles with fried curry leaves.

ingredients.item: 1 1/4 lb Kirkwood boneless chicken thighs, cut into large bite-size pieces
1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste (or 4 cloves garlic and a thumb of ginger, grated)
2 tsp Kashmiri chili powder or sweet paprika
3 tbsp Friendly Farms plain Greek yogurt
Coconut or olive oil, kosher salt

steps.text: Toss the chicken with the yogurt, turmeric, half the chili powder, and a big pinch of salt until every piece is slicked yellow. Leave it on the counter for 10 minutes while you prep everything else.

Toast the peppercorns, fennel, and coriander in a dry skillet over medium for 2 minutes, shaking constantly, until the fennel darkens a shade and the pepper smells sharp and piney. Crush them coarsely in a mortar or under the bottom of a heavy pan.
steps.tip: Coarse, not powdered — you want to bite into the pepper.

steps.text: Wipe the pan, add 2 tbsp coconut oil, and heat over medium-high. Strip in the curry leaves and stand back for 1 minute while they crackle, curl, and turn glassy.
Add the sliced onion with a pinch of salt and cook for 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until it collapses and the edges go deep brown. Crush the rest of your spices while you wait.
Stir in the ginger-garlic paste and the remaining chili powder and cook 1 minute, until the raw garlic smell burns off and the oil at the edge of the pan turns red.
Spread the marinated chicken into a single layer and leave it completely alone for 5 minutes, until the undersides are browned and release from the pan without tearing.
steps.tip: Resist stirring — that first sear is where the flavor lives.

steps.text: Add the tomato and two-thirds of the crushed pepper masala with a splash of water, cover, and cook 10 minutes until the tomato collapses into the sauce and the chicken is opaque throughout.

Uncover, raise the heat, and cook 4 more minutes until the sauce is nearly dry and clinging to the meat. Off the heat, stir in the last of the pepper masala and warm the naan directly over the burner or in the hot pan.
steps.tip: Finishing with raw-toasted pepper keeps the heat bright instead of muddy.

swap: If fresh curry leaves aren't available, leave them out rather than substituting dried ones; Simply Nature chicken breast cut into chunks works if thighs are sold out.
leftovers: Holds 3 days refrigerated; loosen with a splash of water in a hot skillet, or roll into an L'Oven Fresh Protein Wrap with yogurt and raw onion.

title: Neapolitan Chicken Pizzaiola with Olives and Torn Mozzarella
blurb: Golden cutlets buried in a garlicky oregano tomato sauce studded with capers and olives, then melted over with fresh mozzarella.

ingredients.item: 2 large Simply Nature Organic Chicken Breasts, halved horizontally into 4 thin cutlets
1 can (28 oz) whole peeled San Marzano-style tomatoes
1/2 cup green or black olives, torn open and pitted
Specially Selected olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper

steps.text: Pat the cutlets bone dry and season both sides hard with salt and pepper. Film a wide skillet with olive oil and heat over medium-high for 2 minutes, until the oil shimmers and thins out across the pan.
steps.tip: Dry chicken browns; damp chicken steams.

steps.text: Lay the cutlets in without crowding and sear 3 minutes, until the undersides are burnished gold and lift cleanly. Flip, give them 1 more minute, and move them to a plate — they should still be pink inside.
Drop the heat to medium and add the garlic and pepper flakes to the browned fond. Stir for 1 minute, only until the garlic turns blond at the edges and smells sweet.
steps.tip: Browned garlic will make the whole sauce bitter.

steps.text: Crush the tomatoes into the pan through your fingers, add the oregano and a big pinch of salt, and simmer uncovered for 12 minutes. It's ready when it darkens to brick red and orange oil pools around the edge. Tear the mozzarella into rough pieces while it cooks.
steps.tip: Rubbing the dried oregano between your palms as it goes in wakes it up.

steps.text: Stir in the olives and capers, then taste for salt — between the two, it may need none at all.

Nestle the cutlets and any collected juices back into the sauce, drape the torn mozzarella over the top, cover, and cook on low for 5 minutes until the cheese slumps into puddles and the chicken is opaque at its thickest point.
Rest it off the heat for 3 minutes, then tear the basil over the top and drizzle with raw olive oil. Serve straight from the pan with torn ciabatta for the sauce.

swap: Chicken thighs or thin pork cutlets slot straight in; in a pinch use Specially Selected pasta sauce, but simmer it hard for 10 minutes with extra oregano first.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days; pile it cold onto toasted bread, or chop and toss with Priano pasta and a splash of the cooking water.

title: Dominican Pollo Guisado with Green Olives
blurb: Chicken lacquered in burnt-sugar caramel and braised down with sofrito, oregano, and briny olives into a sauce you'll want on everything.

ingredients.item: 4 lb Kirkwood bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks
2 tbsp adobo-style all-purpose seasoning (or 21 Seasoning Salute plus garlic powder)
1 bunch cilantro, stems minced and leaves reserved
1 cup pimiento-stuffed green olives, plus 2 tbsp of their brine
1 1/2 lb Yukon gold potatoes, cut into big chunks
3 pouches Earthly Grains long grain rice
Olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper, water

steps.text: Toss the chicken with the adobo seasoning, oregano, minced cilantro stems, the juice of one lime, salt, and pepper until every piece is coated. Let it sit for 15 minutes while you chop the garlic and potatoes.
steps.tip: Getting seasoning under the skin pays off later.

steps.text: Set a wide Dutch oven over medium heat with 2 tbsp oil and the sugar. Leave it alone for 3 minutes, swirling only once, until the sugar melts and turns the color of an old penny and smells like caramel.
steps.tip: Past dark amber it turns bitter — pull it the second it goes copper.

steps.text: Add the chicken skin-side down in batches without crowding and sear 5 minutes per batch, until the caramel and fat have lacquered the skin a glossy deep brown. Move each batch to a sheet pan.
Dump the fire roasted peppers and onions straight from the bag into the pot and cook 5 minutes over medium-high, until their water boils off and they start to sizzle and catch color.
Stir in the garlic and tomato paste and cook 2 minutes, scraping constantly, until the paste darkens to brick and coats the vegetables.
Return the chicken with any juices, add the olives and their brine, and pour in enough water to come halfway up the meat. Bring it to a boil, then drop to a bare simmer, cover, and cook 25 minutes.

Add the potatoes, uncover, and simmer 20 minutes more, until a knife slides into a potato with no resistance and the sauce has reduced enough to coat the back of a spoon. Heat the rice pouches near the end.
steps.tip: Mash one potato into the sauce to thicken it fast.

steps.text: Pull it off the heat, squeeze in the second lime, and shower with the cilantro leaves. Let it settle for 10 minutes so the sauce tightens, then spoon it over the rice.

swap: Bone-in chicken breast halves or Never Any! drumsticks work fine; a diced onion and two bell peppers replace the frozen peppers and onions.
leftovers: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes well; shred the meat back into the sauce and pile it into Casa Mamita tortillas or over more rice.

title: Laotian Larb Gai with Toasted Rice Powder
blurb: Crumbled chicken drenched in lime and fish sauce, loaded with mint and shallot, and made gritty-crunchy with hand-toasted rice powder.

ingredients.item: 3 tbsp uncooked jasmine or sticky rice
1 to 2 tsp toasted Thai chili flakes
3 shallots or 1/2 red onion, sliced paper thin
1 head butter or romaine lettuce, leaves separated

steps.text: Toast the raw rice in a dry skillet over medium heat for 8 minutes, shaking almost constantly, until every grain is the color of weak tea and the pan smells like popcorn. Tip it onto a plate to cool.
steps.tip: This is the whole dish — don't rush it pale.

steps.text: Grind the cooled rice to the texture of coarse sand in a mortar, spice grinder, or under a heavy pan on a cutting board.

Add a few tablespoons of water and the ground chicken to the same skillet over medium-high and break it into fine crumbles with a spatula. Cook 7 minutes, until no pink remains and the liquid has mostly cooked off.
steps.tip: Poaching in a splash of water keeps the meat tender instead of pebbly.

steps.text: Kill the heat and let the chicken sit for 3 minutes so it stops steaming. Slice the shallots and scallions while you wait.
Whisk the fish sauce, the juice of two limes, the sugar, and the chili flakes until the sugar dissolves. Taste it — it should hit sour first, salty second, hot last.
Pour the dressing over the warm chicken and toss with the shallots and scallions until every crumble is coated and the shallots soften slightly.

Fold in the mint, cilantro, and most of the rice powder right before you serve, then taste and correct with the last lime or more fish sauce. Pile it onto a platter with the lettuce leaves and cucumber spears and dust with the remaining rice powder.
steps.tip: Add the rice powder at the last second or it goes soggy.

swap: Ground pork or turkey works just as well; if there's no fresh mint, double the cilantro rather than reaching for dried.
leftovers: Best within 2 days; wake it up with fresh lime and a handful of new herbs, or wrap it in lettuce with cold rice.

title: Swedish Meatballs in Allspice Cream with Pickled Cucumber
blurb: Tender allspice-and-nutmeg meatballs swimming in a silky pan gravy, cut by sharp vinegar cucumbers and a spoonful of lingonberry.

ingredients.item: 1 lb Simply Nature Organic Grass-Fed Ground Beef
1 small yellow onion, grated on a box grater
1 tsp ground allspice plus several scrapes of nutmeg
1/4 cup white vinegar and 1 tbsp sugar
1/3 cup lingonberry or red currant jam
Olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper

steps.text: Shave the cucumber into near-transparent coins and toss with the vinegar, sugar, a big pinch of salt, and the chopped dill stems. Leave it to pickle for 20 minutes, tossing once, until the slices go limp and translucent.
Soak the panko in 1/3 cup of the cream for 5 minutes, until it looks like wet sand and no dry crumbs remain.
steps.tip: This soaked-bread trick is what keeps them soft.

steps.text: Mix the beef, soaked panko, grated onion, allspice and nutmeg, and a generous amount of salt and pepper with your hands just until it comes together. Roll into about twenty walnut-sized balls with damp hands.
steps.tip: Overmixing makes them bouncy instead of tender.

steps.text: Melt 1 tbsp of the butter with a little oil in a wide skillet over medium heat and add the meatballs with space between them. Leave them undisturbed for 5 minutes, until a dark brown crust forms on the underside.
Roll them around the pan and cook 5 minutes more, until browned on all sides and springy to a poke. Move them to a plate.
Melt the remaining butter in the same pan over medium and whisk in the flour. Cook 2 minutes, whisking, until the paste turns pale tan and smells toasty rather than raw.
Pour in the broth in a steady stream while whisking, then the rest of the cream. Simmer 5 minutes until it coats a spoon and a finger drawn across leaves a clean line.
steps.tip: If it tightens too much, loosen it with a splash of broth.

steps.text: Return the meatballs and any juices, cover, and simmer 5 minutes until cooked through and glossy. Shower with torn dill and serve with the drained pickles and a spoonful of jam on each plate.

swap: Half beef and half ground pork is the traditional mix; red currant jelly or even cranberry sauce stands in for lingonberry.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days; reheat gently with a splash of broth so the gravy doesn't split, and serve over mashed potatoes or buttered noodles.

title: Bolivian Silpancho with Fried Eggs and Llajua
blurb: A breadcrumb-crusted steak pounded thin as a tortilla over rice and crisp potatoes, topped with runny eggs and fiery raw chile salsa.

ingredients.item: 1 lb thin-cut sirloin or top round steaks
2 pouches Earthly Grains long grain rice
Olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper

steps.text: Make the llajua first: chop or briefly pulse the tomatoes, chiles, garlic, and half the cilantro into a loose, chunky salsa with the lime juice and plenty of salt. Let it sit and get juicy while you cook.
steps.tip: Leave the chile seeds in — llajua is supposed to bite.

steps.text: Lay each steak between sheets of plastic wrap and pound with the flat of a heavy pan until it's the thickness of a tortilla and nearly translucent at the edges. Season both sides with the cumin, salt, and pepper.
Press each steak firmly into the breadcrumbs on both sides so they stick in one solid layer, then set them on a rack while you cook the potatoes.

Fry the potatoes in a film of oil in a large skillet over medium-high for 10 minutes, turning only two or three times, until they're deeply golden and crisp on the flat sides. Salt them and move them to a plate.
steps.tip: Turning them constantly is what keeps potatoes pale and soft.

steps.text: Add more oil to the same pan and fry the steaks one at a time over medium-high, 2 minutes per side, until the crust is crackly and deep golden. Slice the red onion thin while they cook.
Heat the rice pouches, then fry the eggs in the same skillet over medium for 3 minutes, until the whites are set with lacy brown edges and the yolks still wobble.
Press the hot rice into a small bowl and invert it onto each plate. Lay a steak alongside it and heap the crisp potatoes over the top.
Crown each plate with two fried eggs, scatter the raw onion and remaining cilantro, and spoon llajua over everything. Break the yolks at the table and eat immediately.

swap: If sirloin is out, pound Simply Nature chicken breast cutlets just as thin and bread them the same way.
leftovers: Best fresh, but holds 2 days with the salsa stored separately; chop the steak and potatoes into a hash and top with a fresh fried egg.

title: Caldo Gallego with Chorizo, White Beans, and Greens
blurb: A smoky Galician pot of pork, chorizo, and white beans simmered until the broth turns orange with pimenton and the greens go silky.

ingredients.item: 1 1/2 lb boneless pork shoulder, cut into 1-inch cubes
12 oz Spanish-style chorizo or Never Any! smoked sausage, sliced thick
6 oz Appleton Farms thick-cut bacon, diced
3 cans (15 oz) cannellini or great northern beans, drained and rinsed
1 1/2 lb Yukon gold potatoes, cut into rough chunks
1 lb collard greens, turnip greens, or kale, stemmed and torn
Olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper

steps.text: Render the diced bacon in a large Dutch oven over medium heat for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the fat has pooled and the edges are browning. Lift it out with a slotted spoon and leave the fat behind.
Season the pork hard with salt and pepper and brown it in the bacon fat in two batches, 5 minutes per batch, leaving it undisturbed until a real crust forms. Move it to a bowl.
steps.tip: Crowded pork boils in its own juice and never browns.

steps.text: Add the chorizo and cook 4 minutes, until the edges curl and the fat runs bright orange. Scoop it out and pour off all but about 2 tbsp of the fat.
steps.tip: That orange fat is the color of the whole soup — keep it.

steps.text: Cook the onions over medium for 8 minutes, scraping up the browned bits, until soft and translucent. Stem and tear the greens while they cook.
Pull the pot off the heat, add the garlic and pimenton, and stir for 1 minute so the paprika blooms in the hot fat without scorching.
steps.tip: Paprika burns in seconds over direct heat and turns acrid.

steps.text: Return the pork, bacon, and chorizo, add the broth and bay leaves, and bring to a boil. Drop to a low simmer, cover, and cook 25 minutes until the pork gives easily to a fork.
Add the potatoes and simmer uncovered for 15 minutes, until a knife tip slides through with no resistance and the broth has reduced slightly.

Stir in the beans and the greens a handful at a time, then simmer 10 minutes until the greens are fully tender and the broth is cloudy and rich. Mash a few potatoes against the side of the pot, fish out the bay leaves, and season with salt.
steps.tip: Mashing a little potato thickens it without any flour.

swap: Smoked ham hock or diced ham can replace the bacon, and any sturdy green — kale, chard, even cabbage — stands in for turnip greens.
leftovers: Keeps 5 days refrigerated and freezes for months; it thickens overnight, so loosen with broth and expect it to taste better on day two.
